findings.evidence: The document addresses employees in sections like Eligibility and How to Apply, but sections like line 23 (backup reviewer), line 33 (manager approves), lines 43-44 (finance office), and lines 65-69 (team coordinates, finance office reviews) address internal staff without clear separation.
findings.fix: Reorganize the document to separate employee-facing instructions from internal-process descriptions. Create a distinct section for each audience or clearly label which instructions apply to which reader.
findings.violation: Two distinctly different readers (employees and internal staff) are addressed in the same sections without clear separation, so an employee cannot tell which instructions apply to them without reading the entire document.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.fix: State the main rule first: 'The home-office equipment stipend is available only when all three conditions are met: (1) the position counts as full-time, (2) the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, and (3) the request arrives before the benefit year ends.' Then provide the conditions.
findings.violation: The passage opens with three conditions before finally stating the governing rule in the last sentence, so a reader holding the unresolved conditions in mind has to re-read to understand what the conditions actually control.

findings.evidence: Program Overview describes what publications the office produces (lines 3-8); Eligibility and How to Apply follow logically. However, Terminology Notes (lines 49-51) provides definitions without context; Program Coordination (lines 63-65) and Review Responsibility (lines 67-69) describe internal workflows the reader does not perform. The structure does not match a reader's task sequence: what happens after I apply? (missing until later sections) What do these internal teams do? (not needed by employee).
findings.fix: Reorganize sections in the order a reader actually needs information: Program Overview (briefly), Eligibility, How to Apply (with Required Documentation integrated), Approval Timeline, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions. Move internal-workflow sections (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility) to an appendix or separate internal guide. Place Terminology Notes immediately after first use or in a glossary at the end.
findings.violation: Sections appear in the order convenient for the writer (program description, then workflow), not the order the reader actually needs them (eligibility, steps to apply, timeline, payment details), forcing the reader to mentally reorganize the information to follow their own task.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: Lines 3-5 describe 'The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter.' Lines 59-61 state 'The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period.' The same term 'reimbursement log' appears to describe different concepts published on different schedules.
findings.fix: Clarify whether 'reimbursement log' is one concept or two. If one, consolidate and explain the publication schedule once. If two, use distinct terms for each.
findings.violation: Terms that may refer to the same concept (reimbursement log) are used in ways that create ambiguity, and the document includes what appears to be duplicated content without clear signal that the information is identical or how it differs.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.
